source.title: Explanation, Debate, Align: A Weak-to-Strong Framework for Language Model Generalization

page_placements.theme: What the student takes from the supervisor: error imitation, pseudo-label correction, coverage expansion, complementary knowledge, style

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some empirical details are not stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes stronger pretrained models on labels from weaker supervisors and reports Performance Gap Recovered (PGR), the same core intervention and measure as the original, across new task domains and model sizes.
record.gate_note: The paper describes the GPT4 family and reports some findings only as qualitative trends or aggregates, without naming individual models or supplying plot values. The student-supervisor agreement results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version: agreement is not itself a measure of beating the supervisor. The concept-probe results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper presents its own weak-to-strong runs: strong students fine-tuned on weak labels, scored by PGR, on NLP, chess and reward modelling, plus confidence loss, bootstrapping and generative fine-tuning. Nominally that matches the original's method and measure. However, nearly every reported result restates the original's (Burns et al. 2023) findings almost word for word. The setup is also implausible. Researchers should treat these results as possibly not independent.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that strong models generalize beyond weak supervision, especially on NLP, and that confidence loss helps most at large gaps. They say bootstrapping and generative fine-tuning address chess and reward modelling, naive fine-tuning does not fully recover performance, and reward modelling stays hard. The record should add that the debate/facilitation framework the paper proposes (Φ, D, Ψ) is never evaluated empirically.
record.recipe_differences: The baseline uses a strong pretrained student fine-tuned on weak-supervisor labels and reports PGR, but adds its own weak-supervisor creation process, task-specific classification heads, NLP and chess settings, and two-epoch training details. It also studies auxiliary confidence loss, bootstrapping, and generative fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: PGR varies by task domain, supervisor-student gap, supervisor and student size, and training method. The text reports different scaling directions for NLP, chess, and reward modeling.

fits_no_version.finding: Student-supervisor agreement falls with model size under every method, and least under the baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-to-strong methods reduce how closely the student imitates its supervisor as size grows. Agreement alone does not show the student beats the supervisor.

fits_no_version.finding: 20% of student errors are attributed to overfitting weak-label errors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A minority of strong-student errors come from imitating weak-label mistakes.

record.problems: Individual model names, sizes, task-wise results, sample counts, and most exact PGR values are not stated. Several results are qualitative summaries of figures. Table 2 provides ablation values without corresponding full-method values. The text does not provide the paired-test sample or detailed statistical procedure.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Ensembling weak supervisors, and loss variants other than the confidence loss.
Quantitative size-by-task PGR, and named model sizes. Representation-based predictors of PGR are reported only qualitatively (Figure 4) with no numbers.
Exploitation of what the supervisor can't check, distribution shift, and error correlation between weak and strong models are all untested.

missing.what: Accuracy p-values for each method versus baseline: 0.03, 0.003 and 0.01.
Ablation accuracy without each component: 0.82, 0.80 and 0.85.
Bootstrapping accuracy keeps improving monotonically, unlike the baseline, which flattens.
Linear-probe concept saliency improves after weak-label training (no numbers given).

record.verdict_notes: Serious provenance concerns. Almost every headline result restates arXiv:2312.09390's findings verbatim: PGR above 50% on NLP, the chess decline, reward modelling at most 20%, confidence loss 25% to 80%, generative fine-tuning 10-20% and 30-40%, the bootstrapping-on-chess pattern, and the error types such as 'poor quote selection'. The setup is also implausible. It claims GPT-4-family models spanning 7 orders of magnitude accessed via the OpenAI API with replaced unembedding layers. Reward modelling appears in the results but not among the stated tasks. Table 1 includes regression and multi-class tasks although all tasks are said to be binary. Tables 2 and 3 and the text contradict each other on which method matters most. Verdicts are given as the paper reports them but should be weighted as possibly non-independent of the original.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not give individual model results, exact PGR values for most conditions, or a detailed comparison to a strong model trained on true labels.
Ensembling weak supervisors and loss variants other than the auxiliary confidence loss are not tested.
The paper does not name individual models or provide numerical size-by-task results; representation findings are not quantified in the text.
No direct test of supervisor-blind exploitation, distribution shift, or the effect of weak/strong error correlation.
No theoretical conditions or guarantee are tested.

relation.reason: The paper presents baseline and enhanced weak-to-strong experiments, including PGR and scaling results bearing directly on V1–V3.

tranche.reason: The paper presents strong pretrained students fine-tuned on weak-supervisor labels and evaluated with PGR, matching the original method and measure. The text does not establish that these are merely cited results.

source_check.notes: The paper presents these as its own results; duplication of the original cannot be independently established from the allowed materials. Reward modelling lacks a stated experimental setup, individual model sizes are absent, and Table 3 omits sample counts and pairing units.

statements.correction: Reward-modelling PGR rarely exceeds 20%; authors describe default generalization as poor. Experimental Setup lists NLP and chess only. Individual PGR signs are not reported. V1 label for this study: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The 20% description and setup omission are accurate. This study does not establish absent or reversed PGR, so its contribution does not warrant challenges. Duplication of the original's values cannot be independently verified from the allowed source text.

statements.correction: Models: unspecified GPT-4-family pretrained models accessed through the OpenAI API. Results presented as the authors' experiments. Specific checkpoints and parameter sizes absent. Duplication of original results not established by the allowed source text.
statements.problem: The supplied paper does not establish that its reported GPT-4-family results are restatements of the original. It presents them as its own experiments; independence remains unverified.

statements.correction: Bootstrapping: promising chess results; limited NLP and reward-modelling improvements. V2 label for NLP and reward modelling: limits_scope.
statements.problem: Limited bootstrapping improvements on NLP and reward modelling are accurately reported, but limited improvement does not establish absent or reversed method gains.

statements.correction: This paper presents generative fine-tuning as improving reward-modelling PGR by approximately 10–20%, reaching 30–40% with early stopping. Relative percentage versus percentage-point gain unspecified. Independence from the original remains unverified.
statements.problem: The reported gain matches the numerical description, but the claim that this paper merely duplicates the original cannot be verified from the allowed source text.

statements.correction: NLP PGR generally increases with supervisor and student size; largest-student PGR often exceeds 50%. Chess PGR decreases with student size for a fixed supervisor and with larger capability gaps. Reward-modelling PGR rarely exceeds 20%. V3 label: supports.
statements.problem: The numerical descriptions and reporting omissions are accurate. The limits_scope label misreads V3: differing size and task trends support the descriptive dependence claim.
